mapName: A Learnable North & East Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.name: Albania - Bold Font Signs
metas.note:
• The numbers on speed signs are written in a bold font.

--- NOTE:

  • The font is much thinner on speed signs in Montenegro.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/albania.

metas.name: Albania - Bollards
metas.note:
• Albanian bollards have a black top with a red and grey reflector.
  • The bottom is painted white.

--- NOTE:

  • Italy uses the same kind of bollards.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/albania.

metas.name: Albania - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Albanian chevrons are white on black.

--- NOTE:

  • Within southern Europe this chevron is also used by Italy, Greece, and Spain.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/albania.

metas.name: Albania - Guardrail Endings
metas.note:
• These flat and wide guardrail endings that bend away from the road can often be found in Albania.

--- NOTE:

  • The same endings are found in Italy.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/albania.

metas.name: Albania - Horizontal Bar Poles
metas.note:
• Other, more simple Albanian pole tops will often have horizontal bars.

--- NOTE:

  • If you are not sure between Montenegro or Albania and see these poles, guess Albania.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/albania.

metas.name: Albania - License Plates
metas.note:
• Albanian licence plates either have blue strips on both sides or a single red strip on the left side.

--- NOTE:

  • Albania is the only European country with red on the left side of the licence plate.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/albania.

metas.name: Albania - Rifts
metas.note:
• Rifts can commonly be seen in Albanian coverage, due to poor stitching.

--- NOTE:

  • Rifts are also equally common in Montenegro, and can rarely be seen in various other countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/albania.

metas.name: Albania - RRUGA
metas.note: • The Albanian word for street is rruga.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/albania.

metas.name: Albania - Upside Down Poles
metas.note:
• These pole tops, with an upside down triangle shape, are a good clue for Albania.

--- NOTE:

  • Serbia, Czechia, Slovakia and Romania use similar pole tops.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/albania.

metas.name: Albania - Water Tanks
metas.note:
• You will see a lot of cylinder-shaped water tanks on the roofs of buildings.

--- NOTE:

  • This is less common in Montenegro.
  • Some parts of Turkey also have a lot of similar-looking water tanks.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/albania.

metas.name: Austria - Architecture
metas.note:
• Alpine architecture is common in Austria and other countries in the Alps.
  • Houses commonly have distinct light coloured walls, with wooden elements such as balconies or panelling around the top floor, with dark-coloured wooden roofs that extend outward.

--- NOTE:

  • Germany uses similar architecture in its southern states.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/austria.

metas.name: Austria - Bollards
metas.note:
• Austria uses white bollards, with a black top.
  • The colour of the reflector is (dark) red or dark grey.
  • Many bollards also feature a small nipple-shaped black cap on the top.

--- NOTE:

  • Slovenia and Montenegro use the same bollards, but with bright red reflectors instead of grey or dark red.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/austria.

metas.name: Austria - Chevrons
metas.note:
Austria uses two colour schemes for chevrons:

  • White on red
  • Red on yellow

--- NOTE:

  • Germany mostly uses red on white chevrons, and rarely red on yellow.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/austria.

metas.name: Austria - Einbahn
metas.note:
• These one-way traffic signs, with the word ‘EINBAHN’ written on them, are unique to Austria.

--- NOTE:

  • In Germany there will be “Einbahnstraße” written on the sign.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/austria.

metas.name: Austria - Landscape
metas.note:
• Most of Austria is mountainous and covered in forests.
  • However, some areas in the east and northeast are much more flat and agricultural.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/austria.

metas.name: Bulgaria - Alternating Poles
metas.note:
• This style of pole top, with 3 large, alternating insulators that are shaped like upward facing hooks, is a good clue for Bulgaria.
  • This pole top is probably unique to the country.

--- NOTE:

  • You can also find this pole top with the insulators facing downwards.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/bulgaria.

metas.name: Bulgaria - Gen 3 Winter
metas.note:
• The majority of Generation 3 coverage in Bulgaria was taken during March and April, resulting in very distinct dead-looking “winter” coverage.

--- NOTE:

  • Hungary and Czechia also have a lot of similar dead-looking Generation 3 coverage.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/bulgaria.

metas.name: Bulgaria - Grey Tape
metas.note:
• You can commonly see a small piece of grey tape at the top of the car antenna in Generation 3 coverage.
  • Not all Gen 3 coverage has this tape.

--- NOTE:

  • This can also be seen in Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary, and Romania.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/bulgaria.

metas.name: Bulgaria - Hook Poles
metas.note: • Most poles have small, alternating hook-shaped insulators.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/bulgaria.

metas.name: Bulgaria - Thin Roadlines
metas.note:
• Bulgaria usually has thin roadlines.
  • This is particularly useful to tell Bulgaria apart from Romania, where roadlines are usually much thicker.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/bulgaria.

metas.name: Bulgaria - Town Entry Signs
metas.note:
• Town entry signs have a simple white design and also use both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabet.
  • Like with the directional signs, the two lines of text are obvious, even when seen from far away.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/bulgaria.

metas.name: Czechia - Black Caps
metas.note:
• Czech sign posts typically have thick, black caps.

--- NOTE:

  • While some European countries have similar caps, Slovakia usually does not have them.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - Bollards
metas.note:
• Bollards in Czechia have orange double reflectors on the front and a single white reflector on the back.
  • There are also rarer blue and red variants.

--- NOTE:

  • The only other country with the same design is Slovakia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - Direction Signs
metas.note:
• Czechia uses arrow-shaped directional signs with a filled in tip.
  • Due to the shape, they are recognizable from behind.

--- NOTE:

  • Slovakia has small white arrows instead.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - House Numbers
metas.note:
• House numbers in Czechia are generally written on blue or red signs with thin white borders.

--- NOTE:

  • On the contrary, Slovak house numbers are typically written on white signs with a thin red or black border.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - No Center Lines
metas.note:
• Czechia often has solid outer roadlines, with no centre line.

--- NOTE:

  • While these roadlines can be found in all neighbouring countries, it is notably also common in Germany.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - Pair Houses
metas.note:
• Suburban houses in Czechia are commonly connected in pairs.

--- NOTE:

  • This is less common in most neighbouring countries, including Slovakia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - Pair Poles
metas.note: • Czechia and Slovakia most commonly use wide, round concrete poles, which are quite often attached in pairs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - Railway Crossing
metas.note:
• Czech railway crossing signs do not have a background.

--- NOTE:

  • Slovak railway crossing signs have a white rectangular background.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - Rolling Landscape
metas.note:
• The Czech landscape is fairly rolling, with a lot of hills and altitude changes, but not a lot of tall mountains.
  • Generally speaking, Slovakia has more mountains, but also more completely flat areas.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - Special B-Type Guardrails
metas.note:
• Czechia and Slovakia both use a special kind of type B guardrail, which is wider than the normal type.
  • No other European countries use the same kind.

--- NOTE:

  • While Slovakia occasionally uses other types of guardrails, Czechia is fairly consistent.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - Thin Font Road Signs
metas.note:
• Czech road signs have a fairly thin font.

--- NOTE:

  • Slovak signs normally have a much bolder font.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Denmark - Bollards
metas.note:
• Denmark has a very recognizable white bollard with a yellow reflector and a dark orange stripe.
  • This bollard is unique to the country.

--- NOTE:

  • Belgium has bollards that may look somewhat similar.
  • However, it will never feature the orange stripe.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/denmark.

metas.name: Denmark - Direction Signs
metas.note:
• Denmark has very unique-looking direction signs that are very useful to recognize the country.
  • They are low to the ground and framed by pipes.
  • They are either coloured red and white or blue and white, with a directional arrow incorporated into the background.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/denmark.

metas.name: Denmark - Double "Splitted" Roadlines
metas.note:
• Denmark has all-white road lines.
  • Double middle lines are very common.

--- NOTE:

  • Some other European countries, most notably Poland and Greece, can have double middle lines.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/denmark.

metas.name: Denmark - Landscape
metas.note:
• Denmark is a generally flat country with wide, open fields between towns.
  • Suburban areas are usually open, with space between buildings.
  • Urban cores are more dense and built up.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/denmark.

metas.name: Denmark - Pipe Signs
metas.note: • This signpost, where the pipe frame is bent around the sign, is unique to Denmark.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/denmark.

metas.name: Denmark - Square Roadlines
metas.note:
• Outer road lines often consist of small white squares.
  • These unique-looking lines are a good way to identify Denmark.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/denmark.

metas.name: Denmark - Town Signs
metas.note:
• This unique sign is found when entering a town.
  • When leaving, there will be a red slash through the sign.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/denmark.

metas.name: Denmark - Vej
metas.note:
• Most Danish street names end in “vej.”
  • This is the Danish word for “street.”
  • Street signs most commonly have a blue background with white text.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/denmark.

metas.name: Estonia - Bollards
metas.note:
• Estonian bollards have a round, baton-like shape.
  • They have a rectangular reflector on the front and two circular reflectors on the back.
  • The reflectors can be white or orange.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/estonia.

metas.name: Estonia - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Estonia uses red chevrons with white arrows.

--- NOTE:

  • Russia and Ukraine use the same chevrons.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/estonia.

metas.name: Estonia - Dashed Roadlines
metas.note:
• Outer road lines sometimes consist of short dashes.

--- NOTE:

  • Lithuania also sometimes has short dashes.
  • In addition, Sweden primarily uses short dashes as outer road lines.
  • Sweden's dashes are closer to the edge of the road.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/estonia.

metas.name: Estonia - Kilometre Markers
metas.note:
All Baltic countries use the same blue kilometre marker.

  • However, they can be distinguished from each other by their angle relative to the road.
  • In Estonia, the marker will be perpendicular to the road.
  • It has numbers on both sides of the marker.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/estonia.

metas.name: Estonia - Metal Cap
metas.note:
• Most wooden poles have a small metal cap on top, similar to those found in the Nordic countries.

--- NOTE:

  • Alongside the Nordic countries of Sweden, Finland and Norway, these caps can also sometimes be found in Latvia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/estonia.

metas.name: Estonia - No Border Signs
metas.note:
• Each Baltic country has a slightly different border for its warning and speed signs.
  • Estonian signs have a thin red border, with no white outline around it.
  • The red border extends all the way to the edge of the sign.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/estonia.

metas.name: Estonia - No Reflectors
metas.note:
• Estonia has normal A-type guardrails with no reflectors.

--- NOTE:

  • The other two Baltic countries can have reflectors on their guardrails.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/estonia.

metas.name: Estonia - Square Poles
metas.note:
• You can additionally find a fair amount of square concrete poles, often also with diagonal supports.
  • These are similar to those found in Lithuania.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/estonia.

metas.name: Estonia - Tee & Tn
metas.note:
• The Estonian words for street and road are tänav and tee, respectively.
  • These words are unique to Estonian.
  • Tänav is often abbreviated as ‘tn’.

--- NOTE:

  • The Finnish suffix -tie, meaning street, can look similar.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/estonia.

metas.name: Estonia - Trident Poles
metas.note:
Trident pole tops are somewhat common:

  • This pole top features one insulator on top, and two to the side.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/estonia.

metas.name: Finland - Architecture
metas.note:
• Finnish architecture is mostly modern and utilitarian.
  • Downtown areas tend to be very modern, with lots of apartment buildings and use of concrete.
  • Suburbs mostly consist of freestanding single family homes.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/finland.

metas.name: Finland - Bollards
metas.note:
• Finland has long black-and-white bollards with a rectangular, white reflector on the front and two dots on the back.
  • They can be either round or thin and curved.
  • The black strip is typically diagonal.

--- NOTE:

  • They can look somewhat similar to bollards found in other Northern European countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/finland.

metas.name: Finland - Direction Signs
metas.note: • Finnish directional signs consist of a solid blue background, white text, and a white border with guiding arrows.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/finland.

metas.name: Finland - Full Roadlines
metas.note:
• Where present, outer road lines will always be solid white lines.

--- NOTE:

  • Unlike Sweden and Norway, Finland does not use dashed outside lines.
  • The only exception to this are the Åland Islands in southwest Finland.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/finland.

metas.name: Finland - Gen 3 Autumn
metas.note:
• A lot of Generation 3 coverage was taken in autumn, meaning that trees in this coverage often have distinct fall colours.

--- NOTE:

  • This is significantly less common in Generation 3 coverage in the other Nordics.
  • This means that when you are faced with a tough decision between countries, a fall vibe can be a good clue for Finland.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/finland.

metas.name: Finland - Shitcam
metas.note:
• Google used a weird, low-quality camera in Finland.
  • This camera is known as the official Ari (or “Shitcam”).
  • It has a wide circular car blur, and can be distinguished from Generation 2 by its lack of a sky halo and often somewhat brownish colours.

--- NOTE:

  • Within Europe, Finland is the only country that has coverage with this camera.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/finland.

metas.name: Finland - Snow Poles
metas.note:
• In Finland, it is common to find orange snow poles with a thin white band near the top.

--- NOTE:

  • These are also found commonly in Norway and Sweden, but with a much wider white band, lower down on the pole.
  • They can also have multiple white bands, while Finnish snow poles usually have just one band.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/finland.

metas.name: Finland - Tie & Katu
metas.note:
• Most Finnish street names end in “tie” or “katu.”
  • These are the Finnish words for road and street.

--- NOTE:

  • You may find roads ending in “polku” and “kuja”.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/finland.

metas.name: Finland - Yellow Road Signs
metas.note:
• Finnish road signs have a yellow background.

--- NOTE:

  • Signs in Sweden and Iceland also have yellow backgrounds.
  • Norway, however, has signs with a white background.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/finland.

metas.name: Finland - Yellow Sign Border
metas.note:
• On traffic signs that have a red border, you will find a thin yellow stroke on the edge of the sign.

--- NOTE:

  • You will not see this in any other Nordic country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/finland.

metas.name: Germany - Bollards
metas.note:
• Germany uses these black and white bollards, with white and light-grey reflectors.
  • The reflector will be orange on bollards next to intersections.
  • Many bollards also feature blue attachments on the side.

--- NOTE:

  • Luxembourg uses almost identical bollards, but they have 3 bolts instead of 2 on the reflector.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/germany.

metas.name: Germany - Einbahnstraße
metas.note:
• These one-way traffic signs, with the word ‘Einbahnstraße’ written on them, are unique to Germany.

--- NOTE:

  • In Austria, there will be “EINBAHN” written on the sign.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/germany.

metas.name: Germany - Gen 4
metas.note: • All car coverage in Germany is made with a Generation 4 camera.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/germany.

metas.name: Germany - No Stopping Signs
metas.note: • “No Stopping” and “No Waiting” signs in Germany will often have white arrows drawn on them.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/germany.

metas.name: Germany - Pole Tops
metas.note:
The most common pole tops are:

  • A horizontal bar with uneven hanging insulators.
  • A Triangle pole top.
  • All kinds of T-Shaped pole tops, which can have varying insulator setups.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/germany.

metas.name: Germany - Sign Back Sticker
metas.note:
• You can commonly find black or dark grey sign backs, which are rather rare in Europe.
  • Most signs will also feature this sticker, with an upside-down red triangle on a black rectangle.

--- NOTE:

  • Italy, Romania and Albania also have black sign backs, however landscape should be sufficient to tell them apart.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/germany.

metas.name: Germany - Town Entry Signs
metas.note:
• German town entry signs are yellow with black text and have a metallic frame.

--- NOTE:

These signs can include a lot of useful information too:

  • The town and or city name on the top.
  • The Municipality in the middle.
  • And the county on the bottom.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/germany.

metas.name: Germany - White Sticker Poles
metas.note: • Most wooden poles in Germany will feature a rectangular white sticker.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/germany.

metas.name: Greece - Bollards
metas.note: • Greek bollards are wedge-shaped with almost square reflectors, being red on the front and white on the back.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Greece - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Greek chevrons have white arrows on a black background.

--- NOTE:

  • Similar chevrons are found in Albania, Italy and the UK.
  • Spain has the same colours, but will almost always have either two or four arrows.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Greece - Dark Wooden Poles
metas.note:
• Greek utility poles are primarily wooden, and often have a distinctly dark brown colour.
  • They will often be noticeably taller than in other countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Greece - Double Faded Roadlines
metas.note:
• In Greece you will commonly see slightly faded, solid white double middle lines.
  • This can be used to distinguish it from most other Mediterranean countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Greece - Gen 3 Winter
metas.note: • Greece has a lot of Generation 3 winter and fall coverage, which tends to look somewhat bleak and depressing.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Greece - Harp Poles
metas.note: • These distinctive poletops, which have a metal frame shaped vaguely like a harp, are unique to Greece.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Greece - Small Lamp
metas.note:
• This type of small lamp, attached to the side of poles with a round shade above the light bulb.

--- NOTE:

  • You can also find them in North Macedonia and Serbia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Greece - Warning Signs
metas.note: • Greek warning signs have a red border and a yellow background.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Greece - Yellow Roadlines
metas.note: • Yellow road lines are more common in Greece than any other southern European country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Hungary - 4 Bolt Signs
metas.note:
• Hungarian signs are usually bolted to the sign post using four bolts, going through the sign, in the shape of a tall rectangle.

--- NOTE:

  • This is not common in any other Eastern European countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/hungary.

metas.name: Hungary - Bollards
metas.note:
• Hungarian bollards are black-and-white, wedge-shaped, and typically have a red reflector at the front, and a white reflector at the back.

--- NOTE:

  • Croatian bollards are very similar.
  • They do, however, typically have the reflector closer to the top, and appear somewhat thinner than in Hungary.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/hungary.

metas.name: Hungary - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Hungarian chevrons are white on red.
  • Black-and-white chevrons may also be seen, but are considerably less common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/hungary.

metas.name: Hungary - Kilometre Markers
metas.note:
• These green kilometre markers can be seen along most Hungarian roads.
  • On highways, the numbers correspond to the ones seen on the map in small yellow boxes near exits.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/hungary.

metas.name: Hungary - Poles
metas.note:
• The most common type of utility pole in Hungary is a concrete holey pole, with relatively thin holes going all the way down to the ground.

--- NOTE:

In eastern Europe, Poland and Romania also commonly use holey poles:

  • Polish holey poles typically do not have holes down by the ground, and tend to be relatively thin.
  • Romanian holey poles normally either have much wider, or much taller holes.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/hungary.

metas.name: Hungary - Tall Sign Posts
metas.note: • Hungarian sign posts commonly appear to be abnormally tall, often taller than the Street View camera.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/hungary.

metas.name: Latvia - Bollards
metas.note:
• Latvian bollards have a thin, slightly curved shape.
  • They have a rectangular reflector on the front, and two circular reflectors on the back.
  • The reflectors can be white or orange.
  • The black strip is slightly angled.
  • Bollards often have numbers below the front reflector.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/latvia.

metas.name: Latvia - Bus Stop Sign
metas.note:
• The bus has five windows.
  • Within the Baltics, this is unique to Latvia.
  • The other two Baltic countries have four windows.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/latvia.

metas.name: Latvia - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Latvia uses white chevrons with red arrows.

--- NOTE:

  • Many other European countries, including Lithuania and Poland, use the same chevrons.

However, Estonia, Russia and Ukraine use chevrons with the opposite colour scheme:

  • Red with white arrows.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/latvia.

metas.name: Latvia - Hook Poles
metas.note:
• Latvian poles have distinctive poletops, with hook-shaped insulators, that are arranged in an alternating manner: left-right-left (or vice versa).

--- NOTE:

  • These poletops are much more rare in the other two Baltic countries.
  • They can however appear in some other European countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/latvia.

metas.name: Latvia - Iela
metas.note:
• The Latvian word for street is iela.
  • This word is unique to Latvian.
  • Very rarely, you might see ‘gatve’ in Riga (abbreviated as gat.).
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/latvia.

metas.name: Latvia - Kilometre Markers
metas.note:
• All Baltic countries use the same blue kilometre marker.
  • However, they can be distinguished from each other by their angle relative to the road.
  • In Latvia, the marker will be parallel to the road.
  • It only has a number on one side.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/latvia.

metas.name: Latvia - Thick Red Border Signs
metas.note:
• Each Baltic country has a slightly different border for its warning and speed signs.
  • Latvian signs have a thick red border, with a thin white outline around it.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/latvia.

metas.name: Latvia - White & Red Reflectors
metas.note:
• Latvia has normal A-type guardrails with white or red reflectors.

--- NOTE:

  • Estonia has no reflectors.
  • Lithuania has orange reflectors.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/latvia.

metas.name: Lithuania - Bollards
metas.note:
• Lithuanian bollards are wedge-shaped.
  • They have an orange reflector on the front, and a white reflector on the back.
  • Both reflectors are rectangular.
  • You may find this thin version as well.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/lithuania.

metas.name: Lithuania - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Lithuania uses white chevrons with red arrows.
  • The small single chevrons (pictured here) usually have a red outline on the edge of the sign.

--- NOTE:

  • Many other European countries, including Latvia and Poland, use the same chevrons (though without the red outline).
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/lithuania.

metas.name: Lithuania - G.
metas.note:
• The Lithuanian word for street is gatve, often abbreviated as g. on signs and Google Maps.
  • This word is almost entirely unique to Lithuanian.
  • However, very rarely, you might see gat. in the Latvian capital of Riga.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/lithuania.

metas.name: Lithuania - Kilometre Markers
metas.note:
• All Baltic countries use the same blue kilometre marker.
  • However, they can be distinguished from each other by their angle relative to the road.
  • In Lithuania, the marker will be at a 45° angle towards the road.
  • The sign itself has an L-shape.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/lithuania.

metas.name: Lithuania - Less Forest Cover
metas.note:
• Lithuania has less forest cover than the other two Baltic countries.
  • As a result, the landscape appears more open and agricultural.
  • Your mileage may vary depending on the round however, so use this meta with some caution.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/lithuania.

metas.name: Lithuania - Orange Reflectors
metas.note:
• Lithuania has normal A-type guardrails with orange reflectors.

--- NOTE:

  • Estonia has no reflectors.
  • Latvia has red or white reflectors.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/lithuania.

metas.name: Lithuania - Pole Tops
metas.note:
• Pictured here are some typical Lithuanian poletops.
  • They often have short horizontal rods, on which the insulators are placed.
  • In some poletops, the insulators are arranged in a trident-like shape, with one on top, and two on each side.

--- NOTE:

These poletops are not unique to Lithuania:

  • They can also be found in the other post-Soviet countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/lithuania.

metas.name: Lithuania - Square Poles
metas.note:
• Lithuanian poles are usually square and concrete, and often feature a diagonal support beam.

--- NOTE:

  • While most common in Lithuania, these are also found from time to time in Estonia, and on rare occasions in Latvia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/lithuania.

metas.name: Lithuania - Thin Red Border Signs
metas.note:
• Each Baltic country has a slightly different border for its warning and speed signs.
  • Lithuanian signs have a relatively thin red border, with a thin white outline around it.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/lithuania.

metas.name: Montenegro - Bollards
metas.note:
• The most common bollard is white with a red reflector on the front and a white one on the back.
  • The bollard also has a black top.

--- NOTE:

  • These bollards are also found in Slovenia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/montenegro.

metas.name: Montenegro - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Montenegro uses black on white or red on yellow chevrons.

--- NOTE:

  • Albania uses white on black chevrons.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/montenegro.

metas.name: Montenegro - Mountainous Landscape
metas.note:
• Montenegro is a small, mountainous country.
  • Inland mountains are lush and green, while most coastal mountains have distinct exposed, light coloured rock.
  • Most roads are also only 1 or 2 lanes wide.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/montenegro.

metas.name: Montenegro - Rifts
metas.note:
• ‘Rifts’ can commonly be seen in Montenegrin coverage, due to poor stitching.

--- NOTE:

  • Rifts are also common in Albania, and can rarely be seen in various other countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/montenegro.

metas.name: Montenegro - Rusty Guardrails
metas.note: • Guardrails in Montenegro are often rusted.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/montenegro.

metas.name: Montenegro - Thin Font Signs
metas.note:
• The numbers on speed signs are written in a thin font.

--- NOTE:

  • The font is much thicker on speed signs in Albania.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/montenegro.

metas.name: North Macedonia - Bollards
metas.note:
• North Macedonia uses two types of bollards.
  • One is rounded and very thin, while the other one is wedge-shaped.
  • They both are white and have red or white reflectors, typically on a black surface.

--- NOTE:

  • Croatia uses the same wedge-shaped bollard.
  • Hungary has a similar wedge-shaped bollard but with more white space above the black rectangle.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/north-macedonia.

metas.name: North Macedonia - Dry Grasslands
metas.note: • The general landscape of North Macedonia consists of relatively dry grasslands, and small hills and scattered trees.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/north-macedonia.

metas.name: North Macedonia - Gen 3 No Antenna
metas.note:
• All coverage in North Macedonia is Generation 3.
  • There will never be an antenna on the Google car.
  • Every other country in Europe will sometimes or always have an antenna in Generation 3 coverage.

--- NOTE:

  • The only other country to have no antenna the majority of the time is Serbia, although there will be an antenna sometimes.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/north-macedonia.

metas.name: Norway - Architecture
metas.note:
• Many houses are painted red, which is also typical for Sweden and Finland.
  • Black painted houses are also quite common, more so than in Sweden or Finland.

--- NOTE:

  • Sweden and Finland generally have more red and yellow houses, while Norway generally has more white houses.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/norway.

metas.name: Norway - Bollards
metas.note: • Norway uses thin, curved rectangular bollards with the reflector inside of a black parallelogram.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/norway.

metas.name: Norway - Centered Top Sign Posts
metas.note:
• Street signs will generally be centred on top of sign posts.

--- NOTE:

  • Street signs in Sweden will normally be attached either to the side of sign posts or lamp posts.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/norway.

metas.name: Norway - Chevrons
metas.note: • Norway uses yellow on black chevrons.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/norway.

metas.name: Norway - Guardrail Wooden Posts
metas.note:
• Guardrails often have wooden posts.

--- NOTE:

  • This is not common in Sweden or Finland.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/norway.

metas.name: Norway - Landscape
metas.note:
• Norway is a very mountainous country, with many fjords along most of the coast.

--- NOTE:

  • Finland and Denmark are both mostly flat, while Sweden has a mixture of flat, hilly and mountainous areas.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/norway.

metas.name: Norway - License Plates
metas.note:
• Norway has long white licence plates with the standard European strip on the left.
  • Commercial plates are green.
  • These are often seen on vans.

--- NOTE:

  • Within Europe, green licence plates are most commonly seen in Norway, but also on electric vehicles in Hungary.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/norway.

metas.name: Norway - Long Dashed Roadlines
metas.note:
• Smaller Norwegian roads typically have long dashed white outer lines, while larger roads have solid outer lines and yellow middle lines.
  • The yellow lines have a distinct tinge of orange.

--- NOTE:

  • Sweden only has white road lines, and the dashes on outer lines are shorter than in Norway.
  • Finnish outer road lines are always solid, and middle lines can be yellow or white.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/norway.

metas.name: Norway - Small Dot Roadlines
metas.note: • Road lines will often be made up of small dots of paint.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/norway.

metas.name: Norway - Snow Poles
metas.note:
• Norwegian snow poles are typically orange, with a fairly thin white reflector.
  • The reflector is normally toward the middle of the pole.

--- NOTE:

  • Swedish snow poles typically have a wider reflector slightly higher up, and Finnish snow poles have their reflector at the very top.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/norway.

metas.name: Norway - Traffic Signs
metas.note:
• Norwegian traffic signs have a red outline and a white background.

--- NOTE:

  • Both Swedish and Finnish road signs have a yellow background.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/norway.

metas.name: Poland - Bollards
metas.note:
• Polish bollards have a red strip that wraps all the way around the bollard.
  • This strip has a red reflector on the front (sometimes hard to see), and a white reflector on the back.
  • Bollards sometimes have numbers on them.

--- NOTE:

  • The same design can be found in Zakarpattia Oblast in Ukraine.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/poland.

metas.name: Poland - Double Roadlines
metas.note:
• Poland has all-white road lines.
  • Double middle lines are very common and usually a good clue for Poland.

--- NOTE:

  • Some other European countries, most notably Denmark and Greece, can have double middle lines.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/poland.

metas.name: Poland - Guardrail & Reflector
metas.note:
• Poland has square (normal B-type) guardrails, with circular red reflectors.

--- NOTE:

  • Poland is one of only a very few European countries with this type of guardrail
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/poland.

metas.name: Poland - Pedestrian Sign
metas.note:
• Poland has a unique pedestrian sign.
  • Instead of the usual zebra stripes, it just has a single horizontal line.

--- NOTE:

  • Austria and Belgium also have horizontal lines, but they use two lines instead of Poland’s single line.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/poland.

metas.name: Poland - Poles
metas.note:
• Poland usually has thin concrete utility poles with see-through holes.
  • The holes often do not extend all the way to the bottom of the pole.
  • You can also find round concrete poles.

--- NOTE:

  • Hungary and Romania also have holey poles, but these are wider and more bulky.
  • In addition, the holes extend all the way to the bottom.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/poland.

metas.name: Poland - Town Entry Signs
metas.note:
Poland has two town entry signs:

  • Agreen one with the locality’s name, and a white-and-black one with a stylized urban area.

--- NOTE:

  • Like direction signs, town entry signs use a distinct font.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/poland.

metas.name: Poland - Yellow Warning Signs
metas.note:
• Warning signs are triangular and have a yellow background and a distinct thin red border.

--- NOTE:

  • In Europe, this combination of a yellow background with a thin red border is unique to Poland.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/poland.

metas.name: Romania - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Romanian chevrons are red on white, often with a yellow frame.

--- NOTE:

  • Several eastern and central European countries have the red on white chevrons, however yellow frames are by far the most common in Romania.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - Dashed Roadlines
metas.note: • While there are many types of roadlines in Romania, these outer lines, consisting of short dashes with narrow spaces, can be a good clue for the country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - Large Pole Sticker
metas.note:
• This type of extremely large yellow pole sticker is specific to Romania.
  • Beware that smaller stickers are also common and that both Bulgaria and Hungary can have similar ones.

--- NOTE:

  • The town or city name will typically be written close to the middle of these stickers.
  • In this case Podu Iloaiei is written.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - Painted Poles & Trees
metas.note:
• Trees and poles will often have white painted bottoms.

--- NOTE:

  • This is also common in Ukraine and parts of Russia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - Poles
metas.note:
• The most common types of utility poles in Romania are holey poles with the holes going all the way to the bottom.
  • The holes are typically either quite wide or quite tall.

--- NOTE:

  • Poland and Hungary also both use holey poles.
  • Polish holey poles do not have holes near the bottom and Hungarian holey poles generally have smaller holes than in Romania.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - Thick Roadlines
metas.note:
• Middle lines are often noticeably thicker than average.
  • This is especially useful to tell Romania apart from Bulgaria, which generally has thinner road lines.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - Waystones
metas.note:
• It is very common to see waystones in Romania.
  • They are typically fairly large, with red or blue framing with the road number on the side, or made of actual stone and somewhat rugged-looking.
  • There is also a very small variant which is all white.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - Yield Sign
metas.note:
• This yield sign, with an extremely thick red border, with a thin white outline, is unique to Romania.
  • Beware that different yield signs also exist in Romania.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Russia - Bollards
metas.note:
Russia has three main types of bollards:

  • A very thin type being attached to a stick.
  • One with a black top section.
  • A red vertical reflector below and a German-style bollard.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/russia.

metas.name: Russia - Decorated Windows
metas.note:
• This style of richly decorated window frames is commonly found on traditional Russian homes, especially on log cabins.
  • They are often painted blue.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/russia.

metas.name: Russia - Gen 3 Cars
metas.note:
• Three Generation 3 Street View cars are commonly found in Russia.
  • The two most useful ones for recognising Russia are a black and a white car, both with a long antenna.
  • You may also see a short antenna without a visible car.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/russia.

metas.name: Russia - Large Apartments
metas.note:
• The vast majority of urban housing in Russia are large rectangular apartment buildings made of simple concrete.
  • Newer buildings in wealthier areas appear more modern.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/russia.

metas.name: Russia - Painted Signposts
metas.note:
• Signposts in Russia often have black painted bottoms.

--- NOTE:

  • This is also common in Kazakhstan.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/russia.

metas.name: Russia - Pedestrian Signs
metas.note:
• Russian pedestrian signs have a simply drawn person and three stripes.
  • Signs will commonly have a bright yellow border.

--- NOTE:

  • Ukraine, Lithuania, Mongolia, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan use the same design.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/russia.

metas.name: Russia - Rural Housing
metas.note: • Rural housing in Russia consists mostly of a basic wooden structure with metal roofs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/russia.

metas.name: Russia - Wide Intersections
metas.note: • Along with containing a large number of bollards, many intersections are unusually wide compared to other countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/russia.

metas.name: Serbia - B-Type Guardrails
metas.note:
• Serbia uses B-Profile guardrails exclusively.

--- NOTE:

  • North Macedonia does not use B-Profile guardrails.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/serbia.

metas.name: Serbia - Bollards
metas.note:
• Serbia has a few bollard designs, however most of them will have an off-centred reflector.
  • The bollards are usually flat, with no depth to them.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/serbia.

metas.name: Serbia - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Serbia uses chevrons with a black arrow on a white background.

--- NOTE:

  • Within Europe, these chevrons can also be found in Slovenia, Montenegro and North Macedonia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/serbia.

metas.name: Serbia - No Antenna
metas.note:
• Most of the coverage in Serbia was taken by a Google car with no antenna.

--- NOTE:

  • Other than North Macedonia, almost all of central and eastern Europe has antenna coverage in Generation 3.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/serbia.

metas.name: Slovakia - Big Font Road Signs
metas.note:
• Slovak road signs normally feature a very bold font.

--- NOTE:

  • The font on Czech signs is much thinner.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Slovakia - Bollards
metas.note:
• Bollards in Slovakia have orange double reflectors on the front and a single white reflector on the back.
  • There are also rarer blue and red variants.

--- NOTE:

  • The only other country with the same design is Czechia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Slovakia - Direction Signs
metas.note:
• Slovakia uses blue directional signs, with small white arrows.

--- NOTE:

  • Czechia has large filled in white arrows instead.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Slovakia - House Numbers
metas.note: • House numbers in Slovakia are typically written on white signs with a thin red or black border.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Slovakia - Mountainous & Flat Landscape
metas.note:
• The Slovak landscape varies between very mountainous and completely flat.
  • Generally speaking, Czechia is hillier, but less mountainous.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Slovakia - Open & Grey Caps
metas.note:
• The top of Slovak sign posts are typically either open, have a grey metal cap or a thin black cap.

--- NOTE:

  • Most Czech sign posts have a thick black cap.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Slovakia - Pair Poles
metas.note: • Slovakia and Czechia most commonly use wide, round concrete poles, which are quite often attached in pairs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Slovakia - Railway Crossing
metas.note:
• The Slovak railway crossing sign has a white rectangular background.

--- NOTE:

  • Czech railway crossing signs do not have a background.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Slovakia - Special B-Type Guardrails
metas.note:
• Slovakia and Czechia both use a special kind of type B guardrail, which is wider than the normal type.
  • No other European countries use the same kind.

--- NOTE:

  • While Czechia uses this type fairly consistently, Slovakia also uses other types occasionally.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Slovakia - Wooden Poles
metas.note:
• It is somewhat more common to see wooden poles, and in turn, white concrete supports in Slovakia rather than in Czechia.

--- NOTE:

  • Because there are many variables, it may sometimes be inconsistent.
  • Therefore, this information should preferably be used to help decide between a difficult fifty-fifty.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Sweden - Architecture
metas.note: • Houses in the Swedish countryside are most commonly wooden and often painted with a distinct dark red paint, which is almost exclusively found in Sweden, Norway and Finland.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Bollards
metas.note:
• Swedish bollards are black-and-white, typically with a grey reflector.
  • Reflectors by intersections are commonly orange instead.
  • They can be either wedge-shaped, round, or thin and curved.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Sweden is the only country in Europe whose chevrons have yellow arrows on a blue background.

--- NOTE:

  • While very rare, yellow on blue chevrons also exist in Luxembourg.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Gen 4 Cars
metas.note:
Generation 4 coverage in Sweden features three Street View cars:

  • A red, a white, and a blue car.
  • Each of the cars can be seen with or without a visible antenna.

--- NOTE:

  • Only the blue car is found in Norway, Finland and Denmark.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Short Dashed Roadlines
metas.note:
• On smaller roads, the outer road lines are white and dashed.
  • They are distinctly shorter than the Norwegian dashed lines.
  • In contrast to Norway and Finland, all road lines are white.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Snow Poles
metas.note:
• Snow poles are typically orange, with a tall white reflector slightly above the middle of the pole.
  • Some poles have a second, thinner reflector above the normal one.

--- NOTE:

Finland and Norway both have similar orange snow poles:

  • The reflector on Finnish poles is usually much thinner and very close to the top.
  • Norwegian poles typically have either one or two slightly thinner reflectors, with one commonly being very close to the middle.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Unique Roadlines
metas.note:
• The outer road lines on highways look solid from a distance, but are typically divided into small sections with a unique pattern, which is different from the solid lines in Finland and Norway.
  • Road lines in Denmark can have a similar pattern, however the individual sections should be rectangular.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Yellow Road Signs
metas.note:
• Swedish road signs have a red border and a yellow background.

--- NOTE:

  • Finnish road signs have a thin yellow border outside the red one.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Ukraine - Bad Road Quality
metas.note:
• On average, Ukraine has some of the worst roads in Europe.
  • Most rural roads have lots of potholes, cracks and warped pavement.
  • This abysmal road quality can really help with tough 50-50s with Russia, which generally has somewhat better roads.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ukraine.

metas.name: Ukraine - Red Car
metas.note:
• All coverage in Ukraine is Generation 3.
  • Most of it was made using a red Google car.
  • This car is almost unique to Ukraine.
  • It sometimes has an antenna, and sometimes no antenna.

--- NOTE:

  • You will not find the red Generation 3 car in Russia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ukraine.

metas.name: Ukraine - Town Entry Signs
metas.note:
• Ukraine uses white town entry signs.

--- NOTE:

  • Russia usually has blue town entry signs instead.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ukraine.
